match.reason: The closest bank point, Properties and uses of polymers, covers chain length, branching and cross-links, but it does not teach choosing the monomer, which the new point's brief requires, and its cross-link depth goes beyond this Units 1 and 2 course, so no bank point fits exactly or with small changes.

draft.title: Designing polymers
card: Monomer
The monomer sets the polymer's chemistry. Side groups or functional groups on the monomer decide how strongly chains attract each other.
Chain length
Longer chains have more contact with neighbouring chains, so they attract more strongly. Longer chains usually give a stronger, tougher plastic with a higher melting point.
Branching
Chains with many branches cannot pack closely. Weaker attraction between them gives a softer, more flexible plastic with a lower density.
Chemists choose these three features to match a use. A strong, rigid item needs closely packed chains. A flexible item such as a bag needs branched chains.
draft.remember: Monomer, chain length and branching can be chosen to suit the job.

a.q: A chemist wants a plastic that is tougher and has a higher melting point. Which change to the polymer is most likely to help?
opts: Make the chains longer
Add many more branches to the chains
Use chains that cannot pack closely
Make the chains much shorter
a.why: Longer chains attract each other more strongly, so the plastic is tougher and melts at a higher temperature. More branches stop chains packing closely, which weakens attraction.
a.clue: More contact between chains means stronger attraction.

b.q: Mei Ling needs a soft, flexible film to wrap sandwiches. Which polymer design suits this best?
opts: Highly branched chains that pack loosely
Unbranched chains that pack closely together
Very long chains that pack closely together
Chains that pack as tightly as possible
b.why: Highly branched chains pack loosely, so attraction between them is weaker. This gives a soft, flexible film. Closely packed chains give a stiffer, stronger plastic.
b.clue: Flexible plastics have weaker attraction between chains.

b.best: Highly branched chains that pack loosely

problems.detail: "A flexible item such as a bag needs branched chains" overstates the case. Many thin carry bags are made of HDPE, which has little branching, so a bag does not need branched chains. Better wording: "A soft, flexible film such as cling wrap can use highly branched chains."

check.summary: Both questions are sound and have one clear answer each. One card line wrongly says a bag needs branched chains, but many bags are made from unbranched HDPE, so it should be softened.
